problem: Attention-based VLN agents ignore visual information and give no clear evidence of grounding instruction components to visual objects; the spatial semantic structure of instructions is not modeled explicitly.
motivation: Navigation needs reasoning over both language and vision. Symbolic spatial-language work shows the value of spatial semantics, but its impact on deep navigation agents is unexplored. Modeling instructions as spatial configurations (motion indicator, spatial indicator, landmark) can enforce sequential execution and ground landmarks to detected objects.
key_idea: Split instructions into spatial configurations, enrich them with motion-indicator and landmark embeddings, and use a state attention whose transitions are controlled by landmark-object similarity, then align objects with the configuration to pick the next viewpoint.
insight: The ablation (T1, val-seen) shows the landmark-object similarity score gives the largest gain (SPL 0.54 to 0.59 seen, 0.29 to 0.32 unseen), so explicit landmark-object grounding matters. Gains are mostly in seen environments; in unseen ones, missed detections and novel objects (e.g. 'pottery') hurt because landmarks are aligned explicitly to detector output. State attention visualization shows sequential execution, whereas soft attention skips configurations.
method: Configuration parser: rule-based spaCy dependency parsing splits instructions at verb phrases into spatial configurations, with motion indicators (verb + attached preposition) and noun-phrase landmarks; 85% split accuracy.

Configuration representation: BERT (frozen) + LSTM token embeddings, soft attention pooled at the pseudo-delimiter token, concatenated with GloVe embeddings of the motion indicator and main landmark (1112-d).
State attention: attention over configurations initialized to the first one and updated by a learned controller gamma via discrete convolution (stay/advance), enforcing sequential order.
Landmark-object similarity: the score S_t between landmark and detected object label embeddings, weighted by the previous attention, is fed with h_{t-1} and the attended image into the controller.
Visual alignment: Faster R-CNN (Visual Genome) object features are attended by the grounded configuration, then over images with h_{t-1}, giving the visual decoder input.
Viewpoint selection: LSTM decoder over [C*, I*]; scores by dot product with image features, summed across 3 elevations; softmax over navigable viewpoints.
Training: T1 (Self-Monitor: CE + progress regression) or T2 (EnvDrop: IL+RL), with optional data augmentation; greedy inference.

setting.backbone: LSTM seq2seq with frozen BERT-base embeddings, ResNet image features, Faster R-CNN object features (trained from scratch on R2R)
setting.training_data: R2R train (plus EnvDrop augmentation data for best model); no other extra data
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (ResNet features of 12 headings x 3 elevations) plus top-36 detected objects per view

numbers.evidence: Table 1 row 8 SpC-NAV* (SR/SPL printed as fractions)

numbers_note: SR and SPL are printed as fractions (0-1) in the tables and are kept as printed, not converted to percent.
results: With T2 and augmentation, SpC-NAV reaches val-seen SPL 0.61 (best; vs. EnvDrop 0.55 and Self-Monitor 0.58) but is competitive rather than better in unseen (val-unseen SPL 0.42 vs. EnvDrop 0.44; test SPL 0.44 vs. 0.47). Consistent seen gains with T1 and T2 without augmentation.
limitations: Does not beat EnvDrop/Sub-Instruction in unseen environments; the object detector misses or cannot recognize novel objects, hurting explicit landmark alignment.
Rule-based parser is noisy (85% configuration split, 73% motion, 77% landmark accuracy) and has split and order errors.
